en: The Śrī Rāma Gītā
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Then, having established the supreme glory of the Rāmāyaṇa through his auspicious self— the very essence of all that is auspicious for the world—
the best of the Raghus proceeded with his former conduct.
Just as it was frequented by the most excellent royal sages. || 1 ||
Questioned by the noble-minded son of Sumitrā,
Rāma related auspicious ancient tales;
[he spoke of] the [curse] upon Nṛga, who was intoxicated by wealth.
Then Rāghava spoke of the twice-born man’s state as an animal.
Once, when the Lord Rāma, whose lotus feet were cherished by Ramā, was seated in a secluded place,
the son of Sumitrā, having attained pure contemplation, approached him.
Having bowed with devotion, he spoke, filled with humility.
For you are indeed pure awakening, the self of all embodied beings; you are the sovereign lord, yourself formless,
yet perceived by those with the vision of bliss, O Great-minded One.
For those who are devoted to the constant attachment [of bees] to his lotus feet.
O Lord, I have taken refuge at your lotus feet, which grant liberation from worldly existence and are meditated upon by yogis; just as one easily crosses the shoreless ocean.
Instruct me so that I may cross over with ease. || 5 ||
Then, having heard all those words of the son of Sumitrā,
the remover of the distress of those who seek refuge, with a serene mind, spoke for the sake of pacifying the darkness of the bowed one.
The ornament of the lords of the earth approached him who had taken refuge in the Vedas.
Śrī Rāmacandra said:
Having first performed the rites prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life,
and having thereby attained a purified mind,
one who has previously completed those duties and acquired the necessary means [should proceed].
One should take refuge in a true guru for the sake of attaining the Self.
Action is the respected cause for the arising of the body;
those two, the pleasant and the unpleasant, belong to one possessed of passion.
Furthermore, from that [action] arise merit and its opposite, which in turn produce the body.
Furthermore, existence is spun out like a wheel by means of action. || 8 ||
Ignorance alone is indeed its root cause; therefore, in this injunction, the abandonment of that very ignorance is what is prescribed.
Knowledge itself is most effective in the process of destroying it.
It is taught that neither the action nor that which arises from it is contradictory. || 9 ||
There would be neither the abandonment of afflictions nor the destruction of passion; consequently, defiled karma would arise,
and from that, the cycle of rebirth would likewise remain unimpeded.
Therefore, the wise person should possess both investigation and analysis. || 10 ||
Surely ritual action is enjoined through the mouth of the Veda, and likewise knowledge is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life; thus,
the duty [to act] is enjoined upon every living being.
Furthermore, that [faith] attains the state of being accompanied by knowledge. || 11 ||
The Śruti has also declared the fault in the non-performance of one's duty;
therefore, this must always be performed by one seeking liberation. [Objection: But is she not independent and the performer of her own constant actions?
Knowledge does not depend upon even the mind for anything at all.
For just as a sacrifice, even though its result is real, requires other factors such as the performers and so forth,
so too does knowledge, even when manifested through scriptural injunctions.
It is distinguished by actions alone for the sake of liberation. || 13 ||
Some say thus; these are proponents of discursive thought (*vitarka-vādins*),
and that too is incorrect because it contradicts what has been seen [by the sages] and because action increases due to the conceit of a body (*dehābhimāna*).
Knowledge becomes perfected through the departure of egoism. || 14 ||
The activity of the nature of knowledge, adorned by the pure and radiant expansion of consciousness, is called the final [state];
it arises through all the factors of action and so forth.
Knowledge destroys the entire collection of causal factors and the like. || 15 ||
Therefore, the wise person should abandon all ritual action entirely;
because they are contradictory to knowledge, there can be no combination of the two.
He is ever devoted to the investigation of the Self, having withdrawn the range of activity of all his sense organs. || 16 ||
As long as the notion of a self persists regarding the body and so forth through illusion, one must perform the duties prescribed by the injunctions;
however, having negated all that [notion] with the statements "not this, not this," [one should proceed].
Then, having abandoned even the supreme self, one should abandon all ritual actions. || 17 ||
When the luminous consciousness, which pierces the distinction between the supreme self and the individual self, shines forth within the self,
at that very moment Māyā dissolves instantly.
Together with their causal factors, they are the cause for the continuity of the self. || 18 ||
And how could that [consciousness], which has been utterly destroyed by the authority of scripture, still be capable of producing effects?
[This is because it arises] solely from stainless non-duality.
Therefore, ignorance will not arise again. || 19 ||
If she were not destroyed and were not born again,
how could the thought "I am the creator of this" arise?
Therefore, she is independent and does not depend on anything at all.
Knowledge alone shines forth for the sake of liberation. || 20 ||
That Taittirīya Śruti clearly declares with reverence that renunciation is the highest of all meritorious actions;
and the Śruti of the Vājasaneyins likewise says, "This much [is the Brahman]."
For the sake of liberation from suffering, action is not the means. || 21 ||
However, by means of the equality of knowledge, you have shown that the sacrifice is not an equal illustration;
for the sacrifice is distinct from its fruits due to its many constituent factors.
The opposite is accomplished for one who bows down. || 22 ||
For the notion "I am subject to transgression" is not established as a cognition of the non-Self for one who perceives reality;
therefore, it should be abandoned by the wise whose Self is immutable.
Action performed according to the injunctions as revealed by the ritual rules. || 23 ||
Endowed with faith, through the grace of the guru and by means of the statement "That thou art," one whose mind is purified realizes the identity of the Self and the individual soul.
May he be happy, unshakable like Mount Meru. || 24 ||

For initially, the comprehension of the meanings of the words is the cause for the methodical understanding of the meaning of the sentence; these are the meanings of the words "That" and "Thou," namely the Supreme Self and the individual soul.
And thus, there would be a state of oneness between these two, characterized by mastery. || 25 ||
Having abandoned the contradiction between the manifest and the unmanifest aspects of the two selves, and having grasped their nature as consciousness,
which is purified and characterized through its defining mark;
Then, having [realized] you as one's own self, one becomes non-dual. || 26 ||

Because it possesses a single nature, the "exclusive" (jahat) [secondary signification] is not possible; likewise, the "non-exclusive" (ajahat) [secondary signification] is impossible due to contradiction.
Therefore, this is a "partial" (bhāga) secondary signification, just like the two word-meanings [in the case of "so 'yam"].
The identity of the two terms "that" and "thou" would be logically consistent, being free from fault. || 27 ||
The body, which arises from the fivefold elements such as taste,
is the locus of experience for the fruits of actions such as pleasure and pain;
it has a beginning and an end, and is born of past karma.
The gross limiting adjunct of the self, which consists of illusion.
Subtle, joined with the mind, intellect, the ten sense organs, and the vital breaths, and arising from the unevolved elements,
it serves as the instrument for the enjoyer of pleasure and the like.
The wise know the body to be something other than the self. || 29 ||
Even here, the cause— which is beginningless, indescribable,
and consists primarily of Māyā— is the supreme body; yet, due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it appears as if situated separately.
One should gradually fix one's own self within the Self.
Yet within those sheaths, it appears in various forms through association, just as a crystal stone reflects different colors;
for this unborn, non-dual Self is by nature unattached.
When this is investigated from all sides, it dissolves away. || 31 ||
The threefold activity of the intellect, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas), is also observed here through the distinctions of dream and so forth;
in this world, it is false because it deviates from one another.
In the eternal, supreme, absolute, and auspicious Brahman.
The function of the intellect (dhi) incessantly revolves from the aggregate of the body, senses, vital breath, mind, and the conscious self;
its characteristic is defined by its having ignorance (tamas) as its root.
As long as existence persists, so long does this one arise from existence.
One who has completely rejected everything by means of the valid cognition "not so," and who has tasted in his heart the solid nectar of consciousness,
should abandon the entire world once its true essence has been grasped.
Just as one who has drunk water abandons the fruit [of that action]. || 34 ||
The Self is at no time dead, nor is it born; it neither wanes nor increases, being eternal;
it is devoid of all excellence and consists of bliss.
Self-luminous, all-pervading, and non-dual. || 35 ||
In such a state, which is free from affliction and consists of bliss,
how can existence, consisting of suffering, be perceived?
It appears due to the power of superimposition upon that which is not afflicted.
[The mind] would dissolve in an instant due to the contradiction with the breath. || 36 ||
The wise call that "superimposition" (adhyāsa) wherein one thing is perceived elsewhere due to delusion, just as,
for example, the perception of a snake in what is not a snake.
In the same way, the world [is superimposed] upon the Lord, as it is upon a rope and so forth. || 37 ||
In the conscious self, which is devoid of conceptual construction and illusion,
this first ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) was fashioned;
it is indeed a superimposition upon the Self, the cause of all.
In the stainless, absolute, and supreme Brahman. || 38 ||
For others, cognitions characterized by desire and so forth, as well as passion and so forth, and pleasure and so forth, are always the causes of saṃsāra;
because those [causes] are absent during deep sleep, there is the other state.
For it is indeed manifested to us as the very nature of bliss. || 39 ||
This reflection of consciousness in the intellect, which arises from beginningless ignorance, is called the "light of the individual soul" (jīva-prakāśa);
it stands apart as the witness of the cognition of the Self.
For he alone is the Supreme, who is unlimited by the intellect. || 40 ||
Due to their coexistence in one place, like iron smeared with fire, the reflection of consciousness (cid-bimba), the witness,
and the intellect (dhi) are perceived as mutually superimposed through the force of mutual identification.
And the state of being insentient and sentient belongs respectively to the intellect and the conscious self. || 41 ||
Having gained the experience of knowledge from the presence of the Guru through the words of the Vedas, and having observed that [the Self],
he perceives his own self as abiding within himself, free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
One should abandon entirely all dullness regarding the self.
I am of the nature of light, unborn, and non-dual;
I am repeatedly manifest, exceedingly pure,
a mass of perfectly purified consciousness, and free from all affliction.
I am complete, consisting of bliss, and actionless. || 43 ||
I am eternally liberated, possessed of inconceivable power, beyond the senses, immutable by nature,
and infinite in extent; thus am I perceived day and night by the wise.
I am meditated upon in the heart by those who proclaim the Vedas. || 44 ||
Thus, for one who constantly investigates the Self with an undivided self, pure contemplation will,
through its causal power, destroy ignorance before long.
Just as an elixir, when properly practiced, [removes] diseases... 45.
Seated in solitude, with senses withdrawn, having conquered the self and purified the inner disposition,
one should contemplate the One, having no other means.
He is visible to the discerning, solitary, and established in the Self. || 46 ||
One who dissolves this entire universe into the Self, the Supreme Self which is the cause of all,
remains as the full one, consisting of consciousness and bliss.
He knows nothing external, nor anything internal. || 47 ||
Before entering meditative absorption, one should contemplate the entire world, including all that moves and is stationary, as being nothing but the syllable Oṃ;
for the Praṇava is the designator, and that [world] is the designated.
It is not perceived due to the lack of subtle discernment, not because of a lack of awakening. || 48 ||
The person who is Viśva is indeed the letter *a*; the Taijasa is proclaimed in sequence as the letter *u*;
and Prājña is recited by all as the letter *m*.
It may exist preceded by meditative concentration, but not in reality. || 49 ||
One should dissolve the universal Puruṣa,
who exists in manifold ways within the syllable *du*, into the syllable *ta*; then, having dissolved that luminous [form] into the syllable *ma*.
The second syllable [of the mantra] and at the end of the Praṇava. || 50 ||
One should dissolve even the letter "ma" within the supreme, dense mass of consciousness (cidghana), as well as the cause here, which is the ego-sense (ahamkāra).
"I am that Supreme Brahman, eternally liberated."
Free from the two-fold vision and liberated from limiting adjuncts, he is stainless. || 51 ||
Thus, always cultivating the state of the supreme Self,
satisfied in his own bliss, and having completely forgotten everything else,
he remains as the illuminator of the eternal bliss of the Self.
He is directly liberated, like an immovable ocean amidst the waters. || 52 ||
Thus, for one who has constantly practiced the yoga of samādhi,
whose range of all the senses has ceased,
and who has completely conquered all enemies, I am ever present.
May I become visible to one who has conquered the six qualities within himself.
Having thus meditated upon the Self day and night, the sage should always remain liberated from all bonds,
experiencing the fruits of his past actions while remaining free from egoistic identification.
Thereupon, it dissolves directly into me alone. || 54 ||
Having understood that existence— whether in the beginning, the middle, or likewise at the end— is the cause of fear and sorrow,
one should abandon everything enjoined by the dictates of ritual law.
One should then worship one's own self as the self of all beings. || 55 ||
When one contemplates this [universe] as non-different from oneself, then one becomes non-different from me, the Self,
just as water is in the ocean or as milk is in milk.
Just as wind exists in milk, in the sky, and in the atmosphere. || 56 ||
Thus, if a sage dwelling in the world should perceive in this way, contemplating that the universe is indeed illusory,
he does so because he possesses both scripture and reasoning, and because [the world] has been refuted [by them].
Just as there is a splitting of the moon in the sky, or such things as the confusion of the directions. || 57 ||
As long as one does not perceive everything as being of my nature, so long should one be intent upon my worship,
characterized by faith and exceedingly intense devotion.
I am he who is visible within his heart day and night.
O beloved, having determined this secret— the compendium of the essence of the Vedas— I have declared it to you;
the wise person who contemplates this here [in this world], [attains the highest goal].
He is instantly liberated from heaps of sins. || 59 ||
O brother, if this world that is perceived is seen by you as mere illusion, having abandoned it entirely with your mind,
then your pure consciousness will be permeated by the contemplation of Me.
May you be happy, filled with bliss, and free from disease. || 60 ||
Whoever serves me— whether as one devoid of qualities, as that which is beyond qualities,
or as the very essence of qualities— at any time,
he touches me by means of the dust raised from his own feet.
It purifies the three worlds, just as the sun does. || 61 ||
This entire essence of the Vedas, sung by me alone through the practice of the Vedanta, is a single [teaching];
whoever, endowed with devotion to the Guru, should recite it with faith—
If there is devotion to my words, one attains my own form.
Thus ends the fifth canto of the Uttara-kāṇḍa in the glorious Adhyātma-Rāmāyaṇa, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
